comparison: Both strongly support the behavioral and molecular evidence for PKCδ's specific role in LTM (C22-C25, C30). OpenEval emphasizes the selective impairment across memory types and RNAi validation. Peer review adds C31-C32 (anatomical localization) and notes all three reviewers found the behavioral assays 'thorough' and 'convincing' with 'no apparent weaknesses.'

OpenEval R2 addresses anatomical localization to α/β neurons (C31-C33). Peer R1 includes C31-C32 in their broader evaluation of PKCδ's role. Both support the anatomical specificity, though peer review groups this with behavioral data while OpenEval separates it as distinct evidence for localization.

Both strongly support the δCKAR sensor validation and training-specific PKCδ activation (C26-C29). OpenEval emphasizes pharmacological validation and specificity controls. Peer review explicitly praises establishing 'a new reporter' and notes C33 (imaging data showing activation in α lobes), highlighting methodological rigor across all reviews.

OpenEval R4 focuses on PDK/PDH metabolic regulation (C34-C36). Peer R3 covers broader metabolic mechanism including C35-C36 plus downstream targets (C37-C41). Both support the metabolic gating mechanism, though peer review integrates this with the full PKCδ-PDK pathway while OpenEval separates metabolic regulation from mechanistic linkage.

OpenEval R5 addresses PKCδ-pyruvate linkage via Pyronic sensor (C37-C39). Peer R3 includes these claims in comprehensive evaluation of metabolic mechanism (C35-C41). Both support the direct link between PKCδ and metabolic regulation, with peer review emphasizing the rescue experiment as 'particularly compelling evidence.'

OpenEval R6 focuses on genetic epistasis showing PKCδ functions through PDK inhibition (C40-C41). Peer R3 includes these claims and explicitly describes the rescue experiment logic. Both strongly support this mechanistic insight, with peer reviewer noting it 'counterbalances PKCδ knock-down alone.'

Both support the upstream DAMB-dependent dopamine signaling pathway activating PKCδ (C42-C45). OpenEval emphasizes MP1 activation and mitochondrial PKCδ activity. Peer R4 notes the 'dopamine-triggered cascade' and that the editor affirms 'a clear mechanistic link' between memory and energy machinery. Both accept this connection without critique.

Both support the temporal dynamics of PKCδ activation (C46-C50). OpenEval emphasizes sustained activation matching metabolic upregulation window. Peer R5 notes successful characterization of 'the timeline of PKCδ activation' as part of comprehensive findings. Both evaluations find the temporal profile compelling with no concerns raised.

OpenEval R8 includes C46-C47 as part of temporal dynamics evaluation. Peer R4 includes these claims in upstream signaling pathway evaluation. Both support DAMB-dependent sustained activation, though they group these claims differently in their overall assessments.

Perfect claim overlap (C51-C57). Both strongly support the distinction between single-cycle and spaced training metabolic consequences. OpenEval emphasizes prolonged metabolic activation enabling LTM consolidation. Peer review notes authors 'successfully identify the molecular players that bridge' spaced training requirements with metabolic activity. Complete agreement on this mechanistic explanation of spacing effect.

Perfect claim overlap (C2, C4, C5, C58). Both strongly support the main conclusions synthesizing all findings. OpenEval describes PKCδ as 'the molecular link' unifying cognitive and metabolic constraints. Peer review states 'strength of evidence is exceptional' with 'no apparent weaknesses,' unanimously endorsing the central thesis. Complete agreement on overall conclusions.

Both support the biological context and significance of spacing effect (C1, C6-C8, C82-C86). OpenEval emphasizes conservation across species and metabolic costs. Peer R8 includes these plus prior work (C9-C11, C87-C88) and explicitly acknowledges the foundation from Plaçais et al. Both accept this established context without question.

OpenEval R12 focuses on prior work establishing metabolic and circuit requirements (C9-C11, C87). Peer R8 includes these claims in broader context evaluation. Both support this foundation from Plaçais et al., with peer review explicitly noting the prior findings on energy costs and dopaminergic gating.

Both support biochemical context for PKC signaling (C12-C17). OpenEval notes these are established facts about GPCR signaling and PKC families. Peer R9 includes these in broader biochemical background and notes authors 'dig into the intra-cell signalling,' implicitly accepting this framework. Both treat as uncontroversial background.

OpenEval R14 addresses PKCδ's unique properties (C3, C18, C19, C67). Peer R9 includes C18-C19 in biochemical background. Both support these properties as rationale for investigating PKCδ, though OpenEval explicitly groups C3 with mechanistic properties while peer review treats as general background.

OpenEval R14 includes C3 (PKCδ as sole novel PKC in Drosophila). Peer R12 includes C1 and C3 as definitional context. Both support these basic characterizations, with peer review noting they are 'well-established in the literature' and unquestioned by reviewers.

Both support broader context of PKCδ in mammalian brain (C20-C21, C60-C64). OpenEval emphasizes novelty and potential conservation. Peer R10 includes these plus discussion claims (C68-C71, C73-C77) and notes 'interesting parallel with mammals' and PKCδ as 'potentially valid target.' Both accept contextualization as appropriate.

OpenEval R16 discusses potential conservation in mammals (C65-C66, C68-C71). Peer R10 includes these claims in broader discussion evaluation. Both support the translational relevance discussion, with peer review noting findings 'should interest a large audience' and discussion is 'well conducted.'

OpenEval R17 addresses known PKCδ mechanism in non-neuronal cells (C72-C73). Peer R9 includes C72 in biochemical background. Both support this established mechanism as basis for neuronal metabolism hypothesis, treating it as accepted literature context.

OpenEval R18 discusses context-dependent PKCδ effects (C74-C77). Peer R10 includes these in broader discussion evaluation. Both support this contextualization about PKCδ's dual nature, with OpenEval noting concerns about rottlerin studies and peer review accepting the discussion as appropriate.

Perfect claim overlap (C78-C81). Both support anatomical and functional context about mushroom bodies. OpenEval notes this is established knowledge justifying focus on α/β neurons. Peer R11 notes reviewers don't question these foundational details, implicitly endorsing the anatomical framework. Complete agreement on standard anatomical context.

OpenEval R21 addresses recent work on mitochondrial motility (C88). Peer R8 includes C88 in prior work context. Both support this citation to Pavlowsky et al. 2024 as appropriate additional context, though OpenEval explicitly notes it represents prior work rather than current findings.

OpenEval R20 evaluates C59 as UNCERTAIN, noting that while global PKCδ activation is observed, proposed mechanisms (passive diffusion or mitochondrial hitchhiking) are speculative and untested. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses this specific mechanistic speculation about signal propagation.

OpenEval R11 includes C1 in biological context evaluation. Peer R12 treats C1 and C3 as definitional statements. Both support these basic characterizations, with peer review noting no reviewer questions these well-established points.

OpenEval R2 includes C33 (imaging showing PKCδ activity in α lobes). Peer R2 includes C33 in sensor validation evaluation. Both support this imaging evidence, with peer review praising the FRET reporter methodology and noting PKCδ activation 'to the sensor's saturation only after spaced training.'
